props.title: City 40

sections.content: **City 40 (2016)** (2016) offers a rare glimpse into Russia's closed nuclear cities, following the pattern of shocking nuclear documentaries like **The Battle of Chernobyl** (2006) and **Command and Control** (2016). Director Samira Goetschel gained unprecedented access to Ozyorsk, a secretive city that produced plutonium during the Cold War. Like **Citizenfour** (2014), the film captures real-time danger as the filmmaker and subjects risk severe consequences for exposing state secrets.

sections.content: The closed city documentary genre gained momentum with **Up the Yangtze** (2007), which examined life in cities affected by China's Three Gorges Dam project. **City 40** builds on this tradition while incorporating elements of surveillance state exposés like **The Lives of Others** (2006). The film's protagonist, Nadezhda Kutepova, risks everything as a local activist fighting for recognition of radiation-related health issues, echoing the whistleblower drama of **Silkwood** (1983).

What sets **City 40** apart is its exploration of nuclear nostalgia - residents who take pride in their classified work despite its dangers. This complex relationship between patriotism and peril recalls **Dr. Strangelove** (1964) and documentaries like **Radio Bikini** (1988), which examined the human cost of nuclear testing through a similar lens of misplaced pride and devastating consequences. sections.content: The film's environmental message aligns with other nuclear documentaries like **Into Eternity** (2010), which explores Finland's nuclear waste burial site, and **The Russian Woodpecker** (2015), investigating Chernobyl's lasting impact. Director Goetschel's approach combines investigative journalism with intimate portraits, similar to **Kate Plays Christine** (2016) in its exploration of how to document dangerous truths.
